problems.description: Module-level init_db() runs a destructive schema init as an import side effect; importing app.py (e.g. from a REPL or a second test module that doesn't set DATABASE first) will create/wipe the default tasks.db.
importlib.reload in the fixture is a smell masking that the app structure (import-time DB init) is not natively testable; a create_app() factory or lazy init would remove the need for reload.

datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat() changes created_at's serialized shape from naive 'YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS' to '...+00:00'; a behavior change for API consumers, though it is the non-deprecated form.

strengths: Replaces deprecated datetime.utcnow() with timezone-aware datetime.now(timezone.utc)
Comprehensive pytest suite covering success paths, error paths, ordering, and 404s
Test DB isolated via tmp_path + DATABASE env override rather than touching the real DB
Small, focused, single-purpose commit; follows existing snake_case/type-hint conventions in app.py
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, conventional greenfield-session commit that fixes a deprecated datetime call and adds solid endpoint coverage, with only a minor import-time side-effect smell from the module-level init_db().

problems.description: Hand-rolled JWT (base64url + HMAC-SHA256) carries only a 'sub' claim with no exp/iat — tokens never expire. Should use a maintained JWT library with an expiry claim.
SECRET_KEY falls back to the hardcoded 'dev-secret-key-change-me' when the env var is absent, silently weakening token integrity in non-dev deployments.
token_required catches bare Exception and maps all failures to 'invalid token', hiding internal errors and accepting any malformed payload as merely unauthorized.
Reimplementing JWT primitives (base64url encode/decode, hmac signing, manual padding) instead of using PyJWT adds bespoke crypto code that must be maintained and audited.

Discrepancy flagged: the 0.71 convention score reflects 7 violations but 6 are in files outside this commit's diff (celery_config.py, repositories.py, test_app.py — pre-existing); the sole app.py flag 'Classes should use PascalCase' is not introduced by this diff (no classes added) and appears to be a false positive.

strengths: Coherent feature-addition session: JWT auth + per-user ownership scoping, threaded through every model function and route in a compatible way.
Faithful to the seed's structure — single-file, model-as-functions, comment-separated sections, get_db pattern, so the addition slots into the existing architecture rather than redrawing it.
Proper password hashing via werkzeug.security and constant-time signature verification via hmac.compare_digest.
Backwards-compatible migration: the PRAGMA-guarded ALTER TABLE preserves pre-existing task rows with NULL owner_id instead of breaking existing data.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, pattern-faithful feature addition (JWT auth + owner scoping) that respects the seed's single-file architecture and uses sound primitives, held back only by hand-rolled tokens with no expiry and mostly pre-existing convention violations.

problems.description: The Celery app and the send_notification_email task are defined inside app.py rather than a dedicated tasks/notifications module, coupling broker wiring to the Flask app module; celery_config.py separation is good, but the task definition could live apart.
The check-then-act on previous['status'] in edit_task is not atomic — two concurrent PUTs to 'completed' could both pass the previous-status guard and fire duplicate notifications.

send_notification_email is a print() stub rather than a real email send and the address is synthesized as '{username}@example.com'; acceptable as a demo placeholder, but it is deferred implementation rather than shipped functionality.
result_backend is configured on redis://localhost:6379/0 (same DB as the broker) but no task result is ever consumed, and broker/result share DB 0 which risks key collisions; harmless at this scale.
The eager_client fixture reloads app module on every test (with a redundant 'app_module = importlib.reload(app_module)' reassignment); works, but a single reload + session fixture would be lighter.

strengths: Cleanly isolates Celery configuration (broker, routes, serializers, timezone) in celery_config.py and re-uses the same config object for the app.
Good behavioral test coverage of the new feature: triggers on completion, does not trigger on non-completed status, and does not re-trigger on re-completion.
Tests use CELERY_TASK_ALWAYS_EAGER so the notification path is exercised end-to-end without requiring a live worker.

New helpers (get_user_by_id) and the edit_task change follow existing patterns: 'with get_db() as conn', @token_required, snake_case functions with type hints, and the existing {'error': ...}/404 error convention.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-tested, pattern-consistent integration commit (architectural_fit 0.8) whose 0.71 convention score is mostly pre-existing or false-positive violations (Celery config keys are lowercase by Celery convention, and no classes/constants were added by this diff), while the new code itself is clean.

problems.description: Password hashing (generate_password_hash) moved into the register route handler rather than into UserRepository, so credential-handling logic stays in app.py instead of being encapsulated with the data layer.

Mechanical convention score of 0.71 is dragged down mostly by pre-existing violations in files this commit did not touch (celery_config.py, test_app.py) plus repositories.py module-level constant naming; the app.py 'Classes should use PascalCase' flag is likely a false positive since the diff only removes functions, adding no classes.

strengths: Introduces the repository pattern, cleanly separating all SQLite access from route handlers as documented in the module docstring.
Injects get_db as a dependency, preserving the existing context-manager pattern and improving testability.
Routes keep identical behavior and return shapes (dict rows), so the refactor is behavior-preserving with no API breakage.
No new dependencies added; consolidates duplicated SQL scattered across ~6 model functions into reusable repository classes.
commit_reviews.summary: A behavior-preserving repository-pattern refactor that cleanly separates data access from route handlers; the low convention score stems largely from pre-existing violations in untouched files (celery_config.py, test_app.py), not from this commit's own code.

problems.description: Rate limiting (the headline cross-cutting feature) has no tests asserting 429 behavior; only pagination is covered.
The /tasks response shape changed from a bare list to a {data, next_cursor, total} envelope — a breaking change for existing clients, though internal tests were consistently updated.
flask_limiter import added but no requirements.txt change is visible in the diff.
Limiter storage_uri resolves at import time via a module-level call; the silent memory:// fallback could mask a Redis outage in production, though it is a reasonable defensive default.

strengths: Rate limiting keyed by verified user token with IP fallback and graceful Redis-to-memory storage degradation.
Keyset/cursor pagination using the limit+1 probe pattern to derive next_cursor — no OFFSET, efficient on large tables.
Pagination follows the existing repository-layer pattern (method on TaskRepository consumed by the route).
Comprehensive new tests covering the envelope shape, limit clamping, and cursor traversal, with existing tests updated to the new contract.
commit_reviews.summary: A cleanly layered cross-cutting session (rate limiting + keyset pagination) that respects existing repository/route patterns and is well tested; the low mechanical convention score (0.71) largely reflects pre-existing naming violations in touched files rather than new ones — the 15 added functions are all correctly snake_case with no new class or constant violations introduced.

compounding_issues: Session 1 replaced the seed's ACID-safe SQLite layer with a lock-guarded JSON flat file (threading.Lock only guards single-process read-modify-write), a storage regression every later session inherited — S2 had to write an in-place migration, S4's repository refactor routed store-wide I/O through UserRepository instead of a dedicated store owner
Hardcoded dev SECRET_KEY fallback introduced in S2 (JWT signing key predictable if env var unset) persisted unchanged through S5

Notification business logic (status-transition detection + email dispatch) embedded in the edit_task route handler in S3, and send_notification_email.delay() is a synchronous failure point — broker down turns a successful task update into a 500
No requirements.txt or dependency manifest: jwt, celery, redis, and flask_limiter accumulate as undeclared/unpinned deps across S2-S5
S5's Flask-Limiter defaults to redis://localhost:6379 with no in-process fallback, so the whole API fails closed (500s on every request) if Redis is unavailable
key_decisions: S1: Rewrite storage from the seed's SQLite to a JSON flat-file store with a threading.Lock (deliberate 'no databases' constraint, but a durability/ACID regression)
S2: Add JWT auth with owner-scoped tasks, password hashing, and a legacy-data migration that backfills ownerless tasks to a synthetic 'legacy' user without destroying existing data
S3: Integrate a Celery + Redis async email notification system (celery_config.py, email_tasks.py), extracting shared fixtures into conftest.py for cross-module reuse
S4: Refactor the data layer into a Repository pattern (BaseRepository ABC + TaskRepository/UserRepository), behavior-preserving with all file I/O moved out of app.py

S5: Add per-user rate limiting (Flask-Limiter, JWT-sub keyed, Redis storage) and cursor-based pagination through paginate_for_owner, changing the GET /tasks response contract to {data, next_cursor, total}
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality steadily improved across the arc: tests grew from 10 to 24 to 32 to 32 to 50 with 100% pass rate at every session, and the refactor (S4) and cross-cutting (S5) sessions demonstrably built on the earlier architecture rather than fighting it — the repository layer S4 introduced was the natural seam S5's pagination exploited, and convention adherence climbed from 0.70 (S1) to 0.85 (S5). Architectural-fit scores oscillated (0.75, 0.85, 0.72, 0.85, 0.82) but the trajectory is net-positive, with the S3 integration dip driven by the notification rule living in the route handler. The main drag is accumulated early debt: S1's flat-file storage downgrade set a ceiling the project never escaped, and by S5 the code was failing closed on a hard Redis dependency with undeclared dependencies stacking up.
story_review.summary: A coherent, well-tested five-session build where each stage (greenfield → auth → async integration → repository refactor → rate limiting/pagination) layered cleanly on the prior one and quality trended upward, undercut only by early compounding debt from the S1 flat-file storage downgrade, a hardcoded dev SECRET_KEY, and a growing pile of undeclared dependencies.
